title: Greed is a dog
hook: greed is a dog, falsehood a scavenger, cheating is eating carrion (Sri Rag M1, ang 15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahao, and your line: may I not forget. What did you see that you wanted? Today Guru Nanak names what's doing the wanting, and gives it a very unflattering face. Day six hundred forty-eight.

There's a dog in every neighborhood that knows exactly when the trash goes out. It can be fed an hour ago and still stand at the gate, nose working, eyes on the bag. Not because it's hungry. Because it's a dog. Some of us have met a version of that dog inside: at a buffet, in a sale, scrolling past one more thing nobody needs. One page after the dream house, Guru Nanak names that dog out loud, and he doesn't soften it.
screen: `THE DOG AT THE GATE.` → `NOT HUNGRY, JUST A DOG.` → `GURU NANAK NAMES IT.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 15. Its first lines run, in effect: greed is a dog; falsehood is a scavenger; cheating is eating carrion. Slandering others is putting their filth in your own mouth. Anger is a fire that burns like an outcast's pyre. Then the punch: these tastes and this self-praise, these are my deeds, O Creator. The word for greed is lab, the hungry wanting that's never full. Now, two things to notice. First, the language is harsh on purpose. Guru Nanak takes the insults of his own day, the names a caste society threw at people it looked down on, and throws them instead at the vices. It's the greed that's the dog. It's the lying that's unclean. The Gurus rejected caste outright, and here the shock of those words is turned around: the real lowness, he's saying, isn't in anyone's birth. It's in what a person does. Second, and this is the surprise: the shabad is in the first person. Not you are greedy. Not they are liars. These are my deeds. The Guru speaks the confession himself, so that anyone singing it is saying it about themselves. Nobody singing this hymn gets to point at the person across the hall. The refrain then turns toward speech: speak in a way that brings honor. Those whose deeds are good are called good at the Lord's door. So the dog isn't destiny. A dog can be noticed. A dog can be trained, or at least told no. The first step is just seeing it at the gate.
screen: `LAB: GREED, NEVER FULL.` · `INSULTS TURNED ON THE VICES.` · `THESE ARE MY DEEDS.` · `SPEAK IN A WAY THAT BRINGS HONOR.` · then, large: `MIND THE DOG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch greed once. Sit and think back over today or yesterday. Find one moment when you wanted more than you needed: one more helping, one more purchase, one more scroll, one more bit of credit. Don't scold yourself. Just see it, the way you'd see a dog at the gate. Notice where you felt it in your body: the chest, the hands, the eyes. Then breathe, and let it sit there without obeying it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru to it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Lab, the hungry wanting that's never full: Guru Nanak names it, lying, cheating and slander, and confesses them as his own deeds, so everyone who sings it does the same.
Your line: mind the dog. Today, catch greed once in the act: at a meal, a store, a screen. Notice it, name it, and don't feed it this time. Day six hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its first-person confession, these are my deeds, is sung by the whole congregation about themselves.

original.note: Gurmukhi: greed, a dog; the opening words of the shabad.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of insults.
what it means: a confession: greed, falsehood and anger, named as my own deeds before the Creator.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak inverts caste-coded terms (choohraa, chandaal) to locate impurity in conduct rather than birth, consistent with the Gurus' rejection of caste.
